regular.label: A regular part of daily life

strong.label: A strong presence in daily life

REG.name: Noticing & registration
REG.tagline: How readily the world's details reach you

lead.occasional: Most sensory information reaches you easily. You tend to notice changes, sounds, and details as they happen.
lead.regular: Some sensory information takes a little longer to land, especially when you're focused or the input is quiet or in the background.
lead.strong: A lot of sensory information stays in the background until it becomes big or someone points it out. Your brain sets a high bar for what counts as worth noticing, which leaves more attention for whatever already has it.

REG.meaning: When registration runs this way, ordinary signals such as a name being called, a mess on the floor, or a change in the room can slip past unnoticed. This is not inattention, and it is not a lack of care. Your nervous system simply waits for a stronger signal before it interrupts you, and a mind that is hard to interrupt can also settle deeply into its work.
REG.advantage: You are hard to overwhelm with small stuff, and you can stay absorbed while the world fidgets around you.

occasional: Keep trusting what you notice. Your radar for change is already working for you.
When something does slip past, treat it as information about the environment, not a personal failing.
regular: Make important signals louder: alarms with vibration, visual timers, a hand on the shoulder before speaking.
Ask people to get your attention before the message: your name first, a pause, then the words.
Turn routines into external cues (checklists, launch pads by the door) so you rely less on noticing in the moment.
strong: Route key information through more than one sense at once: say it, show it, and let it buzz.
Agree on a signal with the people close to you that means the next thing they say really matters.
Build the environment to prompt you: labelled zones, visible reminders, and objects left in the path you'll take.

SEEK.name: Seeking & joy
SEEK.tagline: The input you reach for to feel good and settled

lead.occasional: You reach for extra sensory input now and then, but you're generally comfortable at a steady, moderate level.
lead.regular: You actively look for certain kinds of sensory input, such as movement, sound, pressure, or flavour, to focus, settle, or feel like yourself.
lead.strong: Seeking sensation is a core part of how you regulate and enjoy the world. Movement, pressure, sound, and intensity are not optional extras for you. They are how you refuel, focus, and enjoy yourself.

SEEK.meaning: Seeking means your nervous system runs better with more input, not less. Rocking, music, fidgeting, tight hugs, and spicy food are all ways your body organises itself and tops up its reserves. Given room to seek in ways that work for you, this pattern shows up as energy, motivation, and a real capacity for joy.
SEEK.advantage: You know what brings you pleasure and focus, and you approach the things you enjoy with real appetite and energy.

occasional: Notice which sensations reliably lift or settle you, and keep them within easy reach.
Use a favourite input as a small reward or a reset between tasks.
regular: Build seeking into the day on purpose: movement breaks, a pressure or fidget option, a go-to playlist.
Match the input to the moment: firm pressure and rhythm to settle, novelty and speed to energise.
Keep a small kit of reliable sensory tools for places where seeking is harder to do freely.
strong: Front-load big movement and intense input before situations that ask you to sit still.
Design your spaces to feed the need safely: a crash zone, a swing, resistance, bass, cold water.
Frame seeking as maintenance, not indulgence: schedule it the way you'd schedule meals.

SENS.name: Sensitivity
SENS.tagline: How hard and fast input lands for you

lead.occasional: Most sensory input sits comfortably for you. Now and then something bright, loud, or strong stands out, but it rarely takes over.
lead.regular: Certain input, such as sound, light, touch, or smell, lands harder and faster for you than it does for many people, and can shape how a place feels.
lead.strong: Your senses are finely tuned and pick up a great deal. Input others filter out reaches you clearly and quickly, so busy or intense environments can become a lot, fast.

SENS.meaning: High sensitivity means a low threshold. Signals arrive at full volume, with little of the natural dampening other people rely on, which is why a flickering light, a scratchy tag, or a strong smell is more than a minor annoyance for you. The same finely tuned system that makes some places hard also makes you perceptive, detail-aware, and attuned to things others miss entirely.
SENS.advantage: You notice subtle things early: texture, tone, atmosphere, the small detail that is off. Very little gets past you.

occasional: Keep a small toolkit handy for the odd moment input spikes, such as sunglasses, earbuds, or a preferred fabric.
Trust your read of a room; if something feels off, it usually is.
regular: Reduce input at the source before managing your reaction: dim or swap lighting, lower sound, remove the tag.
Carry things that let you turn the volume down anywhere, like noise-reducing earbuds, tinted lenses, or a scarf.
Plan recovery around unavoidable high-input events rather than pushing through and hoping.
strong: Treat sensory load as a real budget: choose which high-input situations are worth spending on.
Ask for changes at the source in the places you spend time: seating away from noise, softer lighting, fragrance-free spaces.
Give yourself full permission to step out or leave early when you need to. A planned exit is a legitimate strategy.

AVOID.name: Avoiding & load management
AVOID.tagline: The active strategies you use to manage input

lead.occasional: You steer around a few specific sensory situations, but mostly you take the world as it comes.
lead.regular: You actively manage sensory load by choosing, adjusting, and planning around input so it doesn't build up on you.
lead.strong: You are a skilled manager of your sensory environment. You plan routes, curate spaces, and make deliberate choices to keep input at a level that works for you, and that takes real foresight.

AVOID.meaning: Avoiding is easy to misread as fussiness, but it is better understood as strategy. When input reliably costs you, steering around it and shaping your surroundings is a sensible, energy-saving response. The planning, the safe foods, and the carefully set-up room all reflect skill, and the care you put into your environment often benefits the people around you as well.
AVOID.advantage: You know what you need and you build it. Designing spaces and routines that genuinely work is a rarer skill than people think.

occasional: Keep doing what works; a few well-chosen swaps can prevent a lot of overload.
Notice which avoidances genuinely help versus which have quietly shrunk your world, and revisit those gently.
regular: Make your adjustments official. Ask for the seat, the lighting, or the quiet room rather than quietly enduring.
Prepare high-load outings in advance: know the exits, the quiet corners, and your plan to leave.
Protect your set-up spaces at home and work; a reliable calm base makes the harder moments easier to weather.
strong: Distinguish adjustments that expand your life from ones that are shrinking it, and get support to widen the tight ones at your pace.
Share your environment-design skills. The systems you build for yourself often help everyone around you.
Pair avoidance with graded, low-pressure exposure only where you want more access, never on someone else's timeline.

INT.name: Interoception
INT.tagline: Reading the signals from inside your body

lead.occasional: You tend to read your body's internal signals clearly: hunger, thirst, temperature, and the early shape of an emotion.
lead.regular: Some internal signals are clear for you and others are quieter, so feelings or body needs can sometimes arrive later or larger than expected.
lead.strong: Signals from inside your body, like hunger, thirst, temperature, and the build of an emotion, often stay faint until they are big. Reading your inside world takes more conscious effort than reading the outside one.

INT.meaning: Interoception is the sense that reports on your inner state, and like any sense it can run loud or quiet. When it runs quiet, hunger, needing the loo, tiredness, or a rising feeling can go unnoticed until it is urgent or overwhelming. This is not a character flaw. It is a wiring difference, and it responds well to external structure and gentle body check-ins.
INT.advantage: Once you learn your body's signals, you understand them precisely, and you can explain them to others in a way many people cannot.

occasional: Keep listening to early signals. Acting on them while they are small is a real regulation skill.
Use your clear body-read to pace yourself: rest and refuel before empty, not after.
regular: Put needs on a schedule instead of waiting for the signal: timed meals, drinks, and toilet breaks.
Try a twice-a-day body scan: a quick check of hunger, thirst, temperature, tension, and mood.
Name emotions using the body first ("tight chest, fast breath") to catch feelings before they peak.
strong: Externalise the inside world: alarms for food and water, visual comfort scales, a feelings-and-body chart.
Build a personal signal dictionary over time by noting what "hungry", "tired", or "upset" actually feel like in your body.
Front-load basics before demanding situations, since you may not feel the warning until it's loud.

ENERGY.name: Regulation, recovery & energy
ENERGY.tagline: What sensory load costs, and how you recover

lead.occasional: Sensory load doesn't cost you much most of the time, and you bounce back from busy days fairly easily.
lead.regular: Busy, loud, or changeable environments carry a real cost for you, and you need genuine recovery time to reset afterwards.
lead.strong: Managing sensory load takes significant energy for you. Busy days, masking your reactions, and unexpected change all draw on a finite battery, and recovery time is how you come back to yourself.

ENERGY.meaning: This pattern is about the overall cost of sensory life rather than any single sense. Holding it together in loud rooms, absorbing change, and masking your reactions all spend energy, and that spend is real even when nobody else can see it. Recognising the cost and protecting your recovery time is what keeps the tank from running empty. Needing downtime is not fragility. It is an accurate reading of what the day asked of you.
ENERGY.advantage: You know how to go still and recover properly, which is a capacity many people never develop.

occasional: Keep an eye on the cost of unusually big days, even if most days feel fine.
Protect a little wind-down time after busy stretches so small costs don't quietly add up.
regular: Schedule recovery like an appointment: quiet, low-demand time after busy events, planned before you need it.
Watch for the after-school or after-work "release," and make the landing soft rather than packed with demands.
Budget change too: even good surprises cost energy, so leave slack in the plan for them.
strong: Treat energy as a budget you spend and refill, and plan the week around recovery, not just output.
Reduce masking where it is safe to. Every reaction held in is energy spent that will need repaying later.
Protect sleep at the source: manage light, sound, temperature, and textures before the day even ends.

strengths.intro: Every sensory profile carries real strengths. These are the ones that stood out in the answers.

17.title: An early-warning system
17.line: You are learning to feel your body's stress signals before they take over, and that is the foundation of self-regulation.

20.title: Deep, immersive focus
20.line: When something matters to you, the noisy world falls away and you can go all the way in. Few people can concentrate like that.

23.title: A space-shaper's eye
23.line: You instinctively arrange light, sound, and comfort so a space works for you. People around you benefit from that skill too.

30.title: A gift for sensory joy
30.line: Certain experiences bring you deep, reliable comfort and delight. Knowing your sources of joy is a real wellbeing skill.

seek.title: Sensory zest for life
seek.line: You reach for movement, sound, and sensation, and you know how to give yourself energy and pleasure. That appetite is worth protecting.

fallback.title: Self-knowledge in the making
fallback.line: Taking the time to map your sensory world is itself a strength. The more you understand your patterns, the more you can build a life that fits them.

cta.headline: Where to from here
cta.body: If parts of this profile are making daily life harder than it needs to be, an occupational therapist can help. Bringing this profile to a first appointment also means you don't have to explain everything from scratch.

disclaimer: This is a free self-discovery tool, not a diagnostic assessment. It has not been normed against other people, and it does not replace an occupational therapy evaluation. It describes your sensory patterns as they look today, and it works best as the start of a conversation.

appendix.header: For therapists and educators: screening information only. This tool is un-normed and non-diagnostic.
appendix.dunnMapping: The Estus Sensory Profile is an original, descriptive instrument. It draws on published sensory-processing theory rather than any proprietary scoring system. Its six scales map onto commonly recognised patterns as follows: Noticing & Registration corresponds to low registration; Seeking & Joy to sensory seeking; Sensitivity to sensory sensitivity; and Avoiding & Load Management to sensory avoiding. Interoception and Regulation, Recovery & Energy are included as contemporary extensions reflecting the field's post-2006 emphasis on internal body awareness, masking, and the energy cost of sensory load. Scores are un-normed scale means (1–5) with descriptive bands only; no normative comparison or classification is implied.
appendix.footer: If this profile is useful, Estus Health welcomes referrals and is happy to collaborate. A full occupational therapy assessment can build on this screening picture with normed measures and clinical observation.
